objective: As the defender, hunt a live attacker through a CloudTrail export: separate benign noise from attacker activity, pin down the source IP and the stolen identity, and see how the attacker blinded your logging. Then write the guardrail that stops it.
successCriteria: You identified the single source IP that performed the attacker's ConsoleLogin, privilege escalation and log tampering
You found the persistence the attacker created and explained why the trail goes silent
You wrote an identity policy that denies StopLogging/DeleteTrail/UpdateTrail/PutEventSelectors on the org trail without breaking day-to-day CloudTrail use
hints: Many of these API calls also appear in normal, benign activity. Look at WHERE each call came from, not just what it was.
lookup-events cannot filter by IP. Look up the log-tampering events first, then use jq on the exported file to pivot on the IP you find.

Search for StopLogging, take its sourceIPAddress, then filter cloudtrail-events.json with select(.sourceIPAddress=="<ip>"). For the policy, add a Deny scoped to the org-trail ARN with an ArnNotLike condition on aws:PrincipalArn for the break-glass role.

range.scenario: You are on the blue team at Acme Payments (account 111122223333). GuardDuty has not fired, but a developer reports that their IAM user dev-bob was used while they were asleep. You have been handed a CloudTrail export of the day's management events from the organisation trail `org-trail`: a mix of ordinary staff activity and an intruder. Your job is to hunt the attacker in the log, work out which identity and which IP they used, show what they did to your logging, and then write the policy guardrail that would have stopped them from blinding you. Use the terminal like a SOC analyst with the AWS CLI and jq; cloudtrail-events.json is the exported file.

tasks.prompt: Which of these CloudTrail events are HIGH-SIGNAL detections that deserve an alert on their own (even before you know who is behind them)?
options: cloudtrail:StopLogging, DeleteTrail or PutEventSelectors on a production trail
sts:GetCallerIdentity, every time it is called
iam:AttachUserPolicy attaching arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess
ec2:DescribeInstances by the ops automation role
iam:CreateAccessKey for ANOTHER user by a principal that is not the identity-automation role
tasks.explanation: Log tampering, self-service admin grants and minting keys for someone else are rare, high-impact actions with almost no benign explanation, so they are good single-event alerts. GetCallerIdentity is called by every SDK and script all day (it is a useful CORRELATION signal, not an alert on its own), and DescribeInstances by an ops role is normal noise.

tasks.prompt: Use the terminal to find who switched off logging. What sourceIPAddress performed the StopLogging call on org-trail?
tasks.explanation: StopLogging is unique in this log and came from 203.0.113.77, which is not in corporate-ranges.txt. That IP also made the failed and successful console logins, so it ties the whole intrusion together. Pivoting from a rare, unambiguous event to an IP is the fastest way to untangle a noisy log.

tasks.prompt: The attacker created a persistent access key so they could get back in. Which IAM user did they create the new key FOR (see requestParameters of the attacker's CreateAccessKey)?
tasks.explanation: The attacker used dev-bob's credentials but minted a key for svc-backup, a service account nobody logs into, so the persistence would survive dev-bob's password and key being reset. Note the benign CreateAccessKey earlier (alice, for ci-runner, from the office IP): the same event name, but a completely different context.

tasks.prompt: Prove the hunt: look up the log-tampering events, then pivot on the attacker's IP across the whole export with jq. Paste the flag from the enrichment line.
tasks.explanation: You started from the most unambiguous event (StopLogging), extracted the IP, and filtered the whole export on it, which exposes the full kill chain in one view: failed then successful login without MFA, discovery calls, a persistence key, a self-granted AdministratorAccess, and finally PutEventSelectors + StopLogging to blind you.

tasks.prompt: Why is there no activity at all in this trail after 14:24:30Z?
options: StopLogging halted delivery of events to org-trail, so nothing the attacker did afterwards is in this trail
The attacker deleted the S3 bucket that holds the logs
CloudTrail only keeps the first hour of an incident
Events from outside the corporate IP range are filtered out of the trail
tasks.explanation: A stopped trail records nothing, so the attacker's later actions are invisible in it until someone calls StartLogging. The StopLogging call itself IS recorded, which is why you can still see it. This is also why PutEventSelectors at 14:23:40 matters: switching to WriteOnly hides read-only calls such as ListBuckets. Use a second trail, CloudTrail Lake, or GuardDuty as independent coverage.

tasks.prompt: Fix the developer role's policy so developers keep normal CloudTrail access (search history, read status, manage sandbox trails) but can NEVER stop, delete, re-point or narrow `org-trail`. Only the SecurityAdmin role (arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/SecurityAdmin) may do that as break-glass. Context key to use: aws:PrincipalArn.

tests.name: Developers can still search event history
Developers can read the org trail's status
Developers cannot narrow what org-trail records
Developers cannot re-point org-trail to another bucket
SecurityAdmin keeps break-glass control of org-trail
Developers can still manage their own sandbox trail

tasks.explanation: An explicit Deny scoped to the org-trail ARN beats the broad Allow, and ArnNotLike on aws:PrincipalArn carves out the one break-glass role. Scoping by Resource keeps sandbox trails usable, so the control does not push developers to ask for blanket exceptions. In production you would put this in an SCP so even account admins cannot remove it.

tasks.explanation: Management API calls arrive on the default event bus as 'AWS API Call via CloudTrail', so a rule on the log-tampering event names fires even though the trail is about to go quiet. GuardDuty finding types are not API names (the relevant one is Stealth:IAMUser/CloudTrailLoggingDisabled), and an S3 object-created rule would fire on every normal log delivery and, worse, go silent once the trail is stopped.

tasks.prompt: The attacker's CLI user agent contained 'kali'. Which GuardDuty finding family flags API calls made from a Kali Linux-style user agent? (Give the finding type, e.g. Category:ResourceType/Name.)
tasks.explanation: GuardDuty's PenTest:IAMUser/KaliLinux finding fires on API calls from a Kali Linux user agent (with sibling findings for Parrot and Pentoo). It is cheap, noisy-free signal, but trivially evaded by changing the user agent, so treat it as a bonus detection and never as the only one.

takeaways: Hunt from the rare, unambiguous event (StopLogging) to a pivot value (source IP), then expand: the same event name (CreateAccessKey, AttachUserPolicy) appears in benign activity, so context decides.
Attackers disable or narrow logging early; alert on StopLogging/DeleteTrail/UpdateTrail/PutEventSelectors, protect the trail with a Deny or SCP, and keep a second independent log source.
lookup-events cannot filter by source IP: export to S3/Athena (or jq) to pivot, and always keep one place where logs cannot be edited by the accounts that generate them.

objective: Run a cloud incident-response tabletop for a leaked access key: scope the attacker from CloudTrail, then contain in an order the attacker cannot step around while preserving evidence, eradicate their persistence, and write the session-revocation guardrail.
successCriteria: You scoped the attacker's activity (assumed role, host access, backdoor user) from CloudTrail before acting
You contained in a safe order: disable the key, revoke older sessions, isolate the host, snapshot, then terminate
You removed the attacker's persistence and wrote a deny that revokes only sessions issued before the incident cutoff
hints: Read the timeline and finding first. What did the attacker do with the key? Start with CloudTrail, filtered by the leaked access key id.

Think about what each control does NOT stop. A disabled key does not kill sessions it already issued; revoking sessions while the key is active lets the attacker re-assume. Don't destroy the host before its disk is saved.

Order: disable key -> put-role-policy to revoke older sessions -> modify-instance-attribute to the quarantine group -> create-snapshot (wait until completed) -> terminate-instances -> remove the backdoor user (key, policy, then user). Then run `tabletop status`.

tasks.prompt: Which containment order is correct for a leaked long-lived access key that has already assumed a role and touched an EC2 instance?
options: Delete the IAM user, terminate the instance, then investigate from CloudTrail
Disable the key, revoke the role's older sessions, isolate the instance, snapshot its disk, then terminate it
Revoke the role's older sessions first, then disable the key, then terminate the instance and snapshot afterwards
Terminate the instance first to stop the attacker's code, then disable the key
tasks.explanation: Cut off the source first (disable the key, reversible), THEN revoke the sessions it already minted, so the attacker cannot simply assume the role again. Isolate the host and preserve its disk before you destroy anything. Deleting or terminating first destroys evidence, and revoking sessions while the key is still active lets the attacker mint a newer session than your cutoff.

tasks.prompt: Scope the incident in CloudTrail. What is the name of the backdoor IAM user the attacker created for persistence?
tasks.explanation: Looking up everything the leaked key did shows CreateUser/CreateAccessKey/AttachUserPolicy for support-temp with AdministratorAccess. Disabling the original key would not have removed this: the attacker would still have a second, privileged credential. Always scope for persistence before declaring containment done.

tasks.prompt: Why do you DISABLE the leaked access key before deleting it? (Select all that apply.)
options: It is reversible if the alert turns out to be a false positive
It keeps the key's metadata (such as last-used) available for the investigation
AWS refuses to delete an access key that has not been disabled first
A disabled key can still be used by the attacker for 24 hours
tasks.explanation: Disabling stops new signed requests immediately, is reversible, and preserves the key and its last-used data for the investigation; you delete it later during recovery once it is replaced. AWS does not require a key to be disabled before deletion, and a disabled key cannot be used for new calls.

tasks.prompt: After you disable the key, why must you ALSO revoke the role's older sessions?
options: Temporary credentials the key already minted via AssumeRole stay valid until they expire, even after the key is disabled
Disabling a key also disables the role it can assume, so revocation is purely cosmetic
Role sessions are tied to the IAM user and die when the user is disabled
Revocation is only needed for roles used by AWS services, not by people or CI
tasks.explanation: STS credentials are independent of the long-term key that created them and can live for hours. Attaching a deny conditioned on the token's issue time kills every session issued before your cutoff while letting legitimate re-authentication (sessions issued afterwards) keep working.

tasks.prompt: What must you take of the instance's EBS volume, and see COMPLETED, before terminating the instance so the disk can be analysed later?
tasks.explanation: An EBS snapshot is a point-in-time copy of the disk that you can mount read-only in a forensic account. Once the instance is terminated the root volume is deleted by default, taking the attacker's tooling, logs and persistence with it, so the snapshot must exist and be completed first.

tasks.prompt: Which of these belong in the RECOVERY phase? (Select all that apply.)
options: Rotate every secret the compromised role could read and issue a new CI credential
Rebuild the web server from a known-good image instead of restoring the terminated instance
Re-enable the leaked key once the attacker's IP is blocked
Restore the terminated instance from the evidence snapshot into production to save time
tasks.explanation: Recovery means returning to a trusted state: rotate anything the attacker could have read, replace the leaked credential, and rebuild from a clean image. Re-enabling the leaked key or putting the compromised disk back into production hands the attacker their access again. The snapshot is evidence, not a restore point.

takeaways: Order matters: disable the key, then revoke the sessions it already minted, so the attacker cannot re-assume; isolate the host; preserve evidence before destroying anything.
Disable before delete: you keep reversibility and last-used evidence; delete during recovery, after the credential has been replaced.
Scope for persistence (new users, keys, roles) before closing: containing only the original credential leaves the attacker's backdoor in place.
Session revocation is a Deny keyed on token issue time: it kills old sessions but lets legitimate fresh ones through.
